--- title: "The 2PL Is a Tiny Neural Network: Does a Bigger One Predict Responses Any Better?" description: | The Rasch and 2PL models are two-embedding networks with no hidden layer. We build them in PyTorch, check them against `mirt`, then widen and deepen them and ask, on 24 IRW tables, whether a neural network predicts held-out item responses any better than the 2PL. Scored with the InterModel Vigorish, the answer is: only where there is a second dimension to find, and a two-dimensional MIRT finds it as well as a multilayer perceptron does. date: today bibliography: nn_irt_data/references.bib format: html: code-fold: true toc: true toc-depth: 2 execute: echo: true eval: true message: false warning: false freeze: true --- ::: {#setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import torch import irw from nn_irt_helpers import (TABLES, GROUPS, GROUP_OF, SHORT, prepare, fit, predict, imv, log_loss, make_models, SEED) from nn_irt_chart import imv_stripchart_html from imvpy import vanilla_imv from IPython.display import HTML, display Rasch, TwoPL, Bilinear, MLP = make_models() torch.set_num_threads(4) plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} This vignette — including the table selection, the PyTorch and `mirt` code, the analysis design, and the writing below — was produced largely by Claude (Anthropic), working from a task specification and with human review. Treat the methodological choices and interpretations accordingly, and check `nn_irt_helpers.py` and `nn_irt_mirt_compute.R` directly if you are relying on the numbers here. ::: ## Motivation A logistic item response model is a very small neural network. The Rasch model takes a person, looks up one number for them ($\theta_p$), takes an item, looks up one number for it ($d_i$, the negative of the difficulty), adds the two, and passes the sum through a sigmoid. In PyTorch terms that is two `nn.Embedding` layers and no hidden layer at all. The 2PL adds a second item lookup, the slope $a_i$, and multiplies before it adds. Once the models are written this way, a question that is awkward to pose in the psychometric idiom becomes the obvious next step: what happens when the network is made wider (more latent dimensions) or deeper (a multilayer perceptron between the embeddings and the response)? Does a neural network predict item responses better than the 2PL? The question is not new. Variational IRT [@wu2020variational] and the recommender-systems literature [@koren2009matrix; @he2017ncf] both treat person-by-item data as a matrix to be factorised and have explored exactly these widenings. What is missing is a comparison on an honest footing: the same held-out cells, the same prior on persons, the same scoring rule, across enough real tables of different kinds to see where a wider network helps and where it does not. That is the contribution here. We build the classical models in PyTorch, confirm that they recover what `mirt` [@chalmers2012mirt] recovers, widen and deepen them, and score every model on held-out responses from 24 IRW tables with the InterModel Vigorish [IMV, @domingue2025imv], which puts every gain on the scale of a bet. Two flexible one-dimensional models from `mirt`, the monotonic polynomial [@falk2016monotonic] and the logistic positive exponent [@samejima2000lpe], join the comparison, because they make the opposite move from the networks: they change the *shape* of the item curve while keeping a single dimension. The short version of the answer is that on a test built to measure one thing, nothing beats the 2PL; where a network wins, the win is a second dimension, and a two-dimensional MIRT finds it as well as a deeper network does. One of the comparisons also turned up an estimator effect that merits comment on its own. ## Data and methods ### Dataset selection We wanted tables that would spread across the kinds of structure a wider network might find, rather than a random sample of the warehouse. The 24 tables fall into five groups, fixed in `nn_irt_helpers.py`: - **Achievement and ability tests** built to measure one thing (a Brazilian medical residency exam, an ENCCEJA Portuguese form, a Dutch listening test, a general intelligence measure, two vocabulary and ability samples). - **Knowledge tests with heterogeneous content** (two COVID-19 knowledge scales, a financial literacy test, the Author Recognition Test), where the items range over topics and a single dimension is a convenience rather than a design. - **Tests with a documented multidimensional structure** (the ECPE grammar test with its three-attribute Q-matrix, a mental-rotation test, a medical licensing exam). - **Personality and clinical inventories** that mix several syndromes or facets in one table (the Woodworth Psychoneurotic Inventory, the NPI, the Taylor Manifest Anxiety scale, the Eysenck EPI, the MCMI, and four more). - **Developmental screeners** (the ASQ and Denver items from the D-score project), which span motor, language and social domains and are age-adaptive, so each child answers only a slice of the items. All are dense and dichotomous. The response values are checked at fetch time rather than trusted from metadata; one candidate, `vocabulary_iq`, turned out to be polytomous despite its metadata and was dropped (and the metadata corrected upstream). Tables with more than 5,000 respondents or 116 items are subsampled to those caps with a fixed seed, so that every fit on the page stays small enough to run on a laptop. ::: {#cell-data .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Fetch, subsample and split the tables"} data = {t: prepare(t) for t in TABLES} sizes = pd.DataFrame({SHORT[t]: {"group": GROUP_OF[t], "table": t, "persons": int(d.pid.max() + 1), "items": int(d.iid.max() + 1), "test cells": int(d.test.sum()), "mean resp": round(float(d.resp.mean()), 2)} for t, d in data.items()}).T sizes ``` ::: {#data .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: `prepare` calls `irw.fetch`, caches the table, subsamples, assigns integer indices, and draws the holdout mask with a fixed seed. Sizes are after subsampling. ### Held-out cells, not held-out people Every model here has a parameter per person. A model cannot predict a person it has never seen, so the usual split by rows (train on some people, test on others) is not available. We hold out **cells** instead: 20% of each person's responses, chosen at random, are hidden during training and predicted afterwards. Every person and every item stays in the training set. The same mask is used by every model, including the `mirt` fits, which see the held-out cells as missing. This is the cross-validation design of the IMV paper, and it is the only one that makes sense when persons are parameters. ### The models, written as networks The four model classes below are the whole of the modelling code. Each takes a batch of person indices and item indices and returns a logit. | Model | Person lookup | Item lookup | Combine | Parameters | On the residency exam | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Rasch | $\theta_p$ (1 number) | $d_i$ (1 number) | $\theta_p + d_i$ | $N + J$ | 3,339 | | 2PL | $\theta_p$ (1) | $a_i, d_i$ (2) | $a_i\theta_p + d_i$ | $N + 2J$ | 3,455 | | MIRT, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf a_i$ ($k$), $d_i$ | $\mathbf a_i \cdot \boldsymbol\theta_p + d_i$ | $kN + (k+1)J$ | 6,794 | | Multilayer perceptron (MLP), $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf v_i$ ($k$) | $\mathrm{MLP}([\boldsymbol\theta_p, \mathbf v_i])$ | $kN + kJ + $ decoder | 6,775 (small), 11,223 (large) | Here $N$ is the number of persons and $J$ the number of items, and the residency exam column counts parameters for the first table on the page (3,223 persons, 116 items, $k = 2$). The decoder of the small MLP has 97 weights and that of the large one 4,545, so even the large network is mostly embeddings: the step from one dimension to two more than doubles the parameter count, and depth adds comparatively little on top. The models are written in slope-intercept form, $a_i\theta_p + d_i$, as `mirt` writes them, rather than the textbook $a_i(\theta_p - b_i)$. This is not cosmetic. In the textbook form the gradient for $b_i$ is scaled by $a_i$, so the difficulties of weak items barely move during training, and a slope kept positive by an exponential cannot fit an item keyed against the trait, which several of the inventories below contain. The slope here is signed and unconstrained. The MIRT model is the compensatory multidimensional 2PL [@reckase2009mirt]: $k$-dimensional person and item embeddings combined by a dot product, which is also a rank-$k$ factorisation of the logit matrix. With $k=1$ it is the 2PL; we use $k=2$. The multilayer perceptron, the plain feed-forward neural network and the thing most people mean by "a neural net", concatenates the two embeddings and passes them through one or more hidden layers of rectified linear units before a final linear layer produces the logit. The interaction between person and item is then no longer constrained to be a dot product; this is the shape used in neural collaborative filtering [@he2017ncf]. We fit two sizes, both on $k=2$ embeddings: a small one with a single hidden layer of 16 units, and a large one with two hidden layers of 64, so that depth is the only thing that changes between them. ### Estimation The PyTorch models are fit by minibatch gradient descent (Adam) on the mean negative log-likelihood plus a $N(0,1)$ prior on $\theta_p$, which makes each fit a maximum a posteriori estimate rather than joint maximum likelihood (the section that follows builds this up line by line). Each model is trained for up to 30 epochs and the epoch with the lowest held-out loss is reported. That is early stopping with the held-out set doing double duty as a validation set; a production comparison would carve out a third split, and we return to what this choice costs in the results. The `mirt` models are fit offline by marginal maximum likelihood [@bock1981marginal] on the same training cells, in `nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`, and each held-out cell is predicted by its posterior-predictive probability: the item curve integrated over the person's posterior on a quadrature grid. Three models are fit this way: the 2PL again, as the marginal-likelihood anchor for the PyTorch 2PL; the monotonic polynomial model, whose item curve is a flexible monotone function rather than a logistic; and the logistic positive exponent (LPE) model, whose item curve is asymmetric. ### Scoring Every model is scored on the same held-out cells by log-loss and by the IMV against the PyTorch 2PL. The IMV converts a log-loss improvement into a bet: if model 0 predicts held-out responses as well as a coin with bias $w_0$ and model 1 as well as a coin with bias $w_1$, the IMV is $(w_1 - w_0)/w_0$, the relative gain in the bettor's edge. The [IMV vignette](imv.qmd) has the derivation and the R package. In Python we use the [`imvpy`](https://github.com/intermodelvigorish/imvpy) package, whose `vanilla_imv` takes the baseline probabilities, the enhanced probabilities and the outcomes, in that order. The definition is short enough to write out, and the helper module does so; the two agree on the first table's held-out cells to the fourth decimal, the residual being how extreme probabilities are clipped. ::: {#imv-check .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} import inspect print(inspect.getsource(imv)) _te = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"] _te = _te[_te.test] _y, _p0 = _te.resp.values, np.full(len(_te), _te.resp.mean()) _p1 = np.clip(_p0 + 0.2 * (_y - 0.5), 0.05, 0.95) # a deliberately better forecast print(f"helper imv {imv(_y, _p0, _p1):.5f}") print(f"imvpy {vanilla_imv(_p0, _p1, _y):.5f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` def imv(y: np.ndarray, p0: np.ndarray, p1: np.ndarray) -> float: """InterModel Vigorish of model 1 over model 0 on held-out cells.""" w0 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p0)) w1 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p1)) return (w1 - w0) / w0 helper imv 0.41904 imvpy 0.41904 ``` ::: ::: ## Building the network, step by step Before the comparison, we write the 2PL as a network from nothing but `torch`, on one table, so that each piece can be seen. The helper module used later is this code with bookkeeping added. ### 1. Long data is already the right shape A neural network consumes one training example at a time, and an item response is one example: a person index, an item index, a 0/1 outcome. Nothing has to be reshaped to a wide matrix; IRW's long format is the network's native input. Three integer-coded columns become three tensors. ::: {#d9918932 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} d = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"] train = d[~d.test] P = torch.tensor(train.pid.values) # person index, 0..n_persons-1 I = torch.tensor(train.iid.values) # item index, 0..n_items-1 Y = torch.tensor(train.resp.values, dtype=torch.float32) # 0/1 response n_p, n_i = int(d.pid.max() + 1), int(d.iid.max() + 1) P[:5], I[:5], Y[:5], (n_p, n_i) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (tensor([1946, 506, 1335, 1109, 3172]), tensor([0, 0, 0, 0, 0]), tensor([0., 0., 0., 0., 0.]), (3223, 116)) ``` ::: ::: ### 2. An embedding is a lookup table of parameters `nn.Embedding(n, k)` is an $n \times k$ table of trainable numbers. Indexing it with a tensor of integers returns the matching rows. A person embedding of width 1 is a column of $\theta_p$; an item embedding of width 1 is a column of $d_i$. There is no "input layer" in the usual sense: the index *is* the input. ::: {#94d49bca .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} import torch.nn as nn theta = nn.Embedding(n_p, 1) # one number per person theta.weight.shape, theta(P[:3]) # rows for the first three training cells ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (torch.Size([3223, 1]), tensor([[-1.7830], [ 0.0773], [ 1.5723]], grad_fn=)) ``` ::: ::: ### 3. The forward pass is the item response function For the 2PL the logit is $a_i \theta_p + d_i$: look up three numbers and combine them. A `Module` packages the lookups and the combination, and its `forward` method is the item response function on the logit scale. The sigmoid that turns a logit into a probability is folded into the loss below, which is numerically safer than applying it here. ::: {#f41334c2 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} class TwoPLNet(nn.Module): def __init__(self, n_persons, n_items): super().__init__() self.theta = nn.Embedding(n_persons, 1) # person ability self.a = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) # item slope (signed) self.d = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) # item intercept (= -a * difficulty) nn.init.normal_(self.theta.weight, std=0.1) nn.init.ones_(self.a.weight) nn.init.zeros_(self.d.weight) def forward(self, p, i): return (self.a(i) * self.theta(p) + self.d(i)).squeeze(-1) net = TwoPLNet(n_p, n_i) logits = net(P[:5], I[:5]) logits, torch.sigmoid(logits) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (tensor([ 0.0032, 0.0183, 0.0421, -0.0713, -0.1496], grad_fn=), tensor([0.5008, 0.5046, 0.5105, 0.4822, 0.4627], grad_fn=)) ``` ::: ::: At initialisation every item has slope 1 and intercept 0 and every person is near 0, so every probability is about one half. ### 4. The loss is the negative log-likelihood `BCEWithLogitsLoss` is $-\frac{1}{n}\sum_c \big[y_c \log p_c + (1-y_c)\log(1-p_c)\big]$ with $p_c = \sigma(\text{logit}_c)$: the mean negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model, which is exactly the quantity an IRT package maximises. Before training it is $\log 2 \approx 0.693$, the log-loss of a fair coin. ::: {#259d8de2 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() loss_fn(net(P, I), Y).item() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 0.6944198608398438 ``` ::: ::: ### 5. A prior on persons, but not on items Persons and items are both parameters here, but they are not in the same position. Each item is answered by thousands of persons, so its slope and intercept are pinned down by the data and need no help. Each person answers a dozen to a hundred items, and there is a new $\theta_p$ for every person added to the sample, so the person parameters never stop multiplying. Fitting a free $\theta_p$ for every person by maximum likelihood is joint maximum likelihood, which is inconsistent as the number of persons grows [@haberman1977maximum] and runs away for perfect scores. IRT software avoids this by integrating $\theta$ out under a $N(0,1)$ prior, which is marginal maximum likelihood [@bock1981marginal]; the item parameters are left as free fixed effects, exactly as they are here. The network's equivalent is to add $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_p \theta_p^2$ to the loss, scaled by $1/n$ to match the mean log-likelihood. That makes the fit a MAP estimate under the same normal prior, and it is a single line. Nothing here puts a prior on the item slopes, and the networks do not need one for the comparison. ::: {#ce6cac2c .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} def objective(net, p, i, y, n=len(train)): nll = loss_fn(net(p, i), y) prior = 0.5 * (net.theta(p) ** 2).sum() / n # N(0,1) prior on theta return nll + prior ``` ::: (The helper module spreads the prior over each person's responses so that it is unbiased in a minibatch; the idea is the same.) ### 6. The training loop Gradient descent on the objective, in minibatches, with Adam as the optimiser. Each pass over the training cells is an epoch. This is the whole algorithm; everything else is monitoring. ::: {#92e99f92 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} torch.manual_seed(SEED) opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=0.02) n, batch = len(train), 4096 for epoch in range(10): perm = torch.randperm(n) for s in range(0, n, batch): j = perm[s:s + batch] opt.zero_grad() objective(net, P[j], I[j], Y[j]).backward() opt.step() with torch.no_grad(): print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:2d} train log-loss {loss_fn(net(P, I), Y).item():.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` epoch 1 train log-loss 0.5570 epoch 2 train log-loss 0.5430 epoch 3 train log-loss 0.5409 epoch 4 train log-loss 0.5402 epoch 5 train log-loss 0.5399 epoch 6 train log-loss 0.5398 epoch 7 train log-loss 0.5398 epoch 8 train log-loss 0.5397 epoch 9 train log-loss 0.5397 epoch 10 train log-loss 0.5397 ``` ::: ::: Ten epochs take a few seconds on a laptop CPU, and the training log-loss settles at the value the 2PL can reach on this table. Held-out predictions are the same forward pass on the held-out indices, through a sigmoid: ::: {#fb3d357e .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} test = d[d.test] with torch.no_grad(): p_test = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(test.pid.values), torch.tensor(test.iid.values))).numpy() log_loss(test.resp.values, p_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` 0.5479466021815232 ``` ::: ::: That is a complete item response model, fit by a neural-network toolkit, in about thirty lines. The Rasch model drops the slope. The multidimensional model makes the embeddings wider. The MLP replaces the dot product with hidden layers. All four live in the helper module with the same training loop (`fit`), which also records train and held-out loss per epoch. ## Results ### The network recovers what mirt recovers First, the Rasch and 2PL models from the helper module, trained with the same loop as above on the residency exam, each reported by its training and held-out log-loss after the final epoch. The 2PL's held-out loss is the number to carry forward: everything else on the page is scored against it. ::: {#fit-one .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Fit Rasch and 2PL on the residency exam"} rasch, h_rasch = fit(Rasch(n_p, n_i), d) twopl, h_2pl = fit(TwoPL(n_p, n_i), d) for name, h in (("Rasch", h_rasch), ("2PL", h_2pl)): last = h.iloc[-1] print(f"{name:6s} after {int(last.epoch)} epochs: " f"train log-loss {last.train:.4f}, held-out log-loss {last.test:.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rasch after 80 epochs: train log-loss 0.5495, held-out log-loss 0.5576 2PL after 80 epochs: train log-loss 0.5396, held-out log-loss 0.5478 ``` ::: ::: Does the network recover the item parameters? The offline `mirt` 2PL fit wrote its slopes and intercepts next to its predictions, so we can compare item by item. ::: {#cell-fig-recovery .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Item parameters: PyTorch against mirt"} ref = pd.read_csv("nn_irt_data/borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt_mirt_2pl_items.csv", dtype={"item": str}) ref = ref.set_index("item").reindex(sorted(d["item"].unique())) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4)) ax[0].scatter(ref.d, twopl.d.weight.detach().numpy().ravel(), s=12) ax[0].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL intercept $d$", ylabel="PyTorch 2PL intercept $d$") sd_theta = twopl.theta.weight.detach().numpy().std() ax[1].scatter(ref.a, twopl.a.weight.detach().numpy().ravel() * sd_theta, s=12) ax[1].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL slope $a$", ylabel=r"PyTorch 2PL slope $a \times \mathrm{sd}(\hat\theta)$") for a_ in ax: lo, hi = a_.get_xlim(); a_.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], "k--", lw=0.8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-recovery-output-1.png){#fig-recovery width=978 height=428} ::: ::: The intercepts agree to the dot. The slopes agree once the scale of $\theta$ is accounted for: `mirt` fixes the *population* variance of $\theta$ at one, while the network's point estimates are shrunk by the prior and have a smaller spread, so its raw slopes are proportionally larger. Multiplying them by the spread of $\hat\theta$ puts the two on the same footing. The remaining scatter is the difference between a point estimate for each person and integrating the person out, to which we return below. ### Wider networks overfit, and early stopping is the fix Now the models that are not classical IRT, still on the residency exam. Before looking, it helps to say what to expect. Training loss should fall in order of parameter count: a model with more freedom can always fit the cells it is shown at least as well as a model with less, so the Rasch curve should sit highest, the 2PL below it, and the three wider models below that. Held-out loss is a different matter. Extra parameters only help there if they capture something that generalises from a person's training cells to their held-out ones; if they do not, the model spends its freedom memorising the training cells, and held-out loss turns upward after an early minimum. On a test built to measure one thing, the anticipation is therefore that the wider models will win on the left panel and lose on the right, and that the losing will be worst for the model with the most parameters. ::: {#cell-fig-curves .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Training and held-out loss by epoch, five models"} curves = {} curves["Rasch"] = h_rasch curves["2PL"] = h_2pl _, curves["MIRT k=2"] = fit(Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2), d, epochs=30) _, curves["MLP small"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)), d, epochs=30) _, curves["MLP large"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)), d, epochs=30) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharey=False) for name, h in curves.items(): ax[0].plot(h.epoch, h.train, label=name) ax[1].plot(h.epoch, h.test, label=name) ax[0].set(title="training log-loss", xlabel="epoch", ylabel="log-loss") ax[1].set(title="held-out log-loss", xlabel="epoch") ax[1].legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-curves-output-1.png){#fig-curves width=979 height=429} ::: ::: That is what happens. On the left, the Rasch and 2PL curves flatten within ten epochs at the value each model can reach, and the three wider models keep going, ending a full 0.01 below the 2PL in training loss. On the right, the 2PL is the best held-out model at every epoch after the first few. The MIRT model touches the 2PL's held-out loss around its third or fourth epoch and then drifts slowly upward; the small multilayer perceptron does the same with more noise; the large one is at its best around the fourth epoch and by epoch thirty has given back about 0.006 of that, ending 0.008 behind the 2PL and only just ahead of the Rasch model, having fit the training cells better than anything else on the page. The gap between the two panels is overfitting made visible, and it widens with parameter count, as anticipated. Two practical consequences follow. First, the wider models have to be stopped early, and their best held-out epoch arrives fast, after three to five passes over the data, so every model in the comparison below is reported at its best held-out epoch rather than at convergence. Second, the test length matters: a person with 93 training responses, as here, pins their $\theta_p$ down well enough that the 2PL barely overfits at all, which is why its held-out curve is flat. ``` ::: ::: ### On tests built to measure one thing, nothing beats the 2PL Across the achievement and ability tests, the knowledge tests and two of the three exams with a documented multidimensional structure, the wider networks sit within about 0.01 IMV of the 2PL, and as often below it as above. For calibration, the IMV paper puts the gain from 1PL to 2PL on typical cognitive data at roughly the value of knowing someone's age when predicting chronic disease; the gains here are a fraction of that, and they go both ways. The ECPE grammar test is the instructive case. It has a known three-attribute Q-matrix, and a model built to find structure still predicts no better, because the attributes are too correlated to carry separate signal in held-out cells. Structure that is real in the design can be invisible in prediction. The one clear exception in this group is the FSIQ mental-rotation test, where every wider network gains about 0.03, which says the test is not unidimensional in practice whatever it was built to measure. ### Where the networks win, the win is multidimensionality, and MIRT captures it The gains cluster in the personality and clinical inventories: about 0.03 on the ADQ anhedonia scale, 0.02 on the Eysenck EPI (three scales in one table), 0.008 on the Woodworth, with smaller gains on the Author Recognition Test and the GMI. In every one of these the MLPs match or trail the two-dimensional MIRT, and the large MLP is never reliably better than the small one. Once the embeddings are two-dimensional, a nonlinear decoder adds nothing on these data. Put differently: the signal a network can find in a person-by-item table of this kind is a second dimension, and a dot product already finds it. Depth is not where the signal is. The Rasch row shows the same thing from the other side. Its large losses (0.11 on the NPI, 0.08 on the ADQ, 0.07 on the Denver screener) are tables where slopes differ sharply across items, including reverse-keyed items a Rasch model cannot fit at all. The step from one item parameter to two is worth more than every step after it. ### Flexible item curves add nothing The asymmetric LPE curve tracks the `mirt` 2PL to within 0.001 on every table. The monotonic polynomial is the same on the tests and worse on several inventories (0.04 below on the NPI, 0.015 on the ADQ), and it failed to converge on three of the longer tables. Changing the shape of the item curve while keeping one dimension is not where the predictable signal is either. Taken with the previous section, the picture is fairly simple: on dichotomous tables, the 2PL's logistic curve is good enough, and the only thing worth adding is a dimension, when the instrument has one to add. ### The mirt 2PL gap is an estimator effect, and it is largest on short tests The same 2PL fit by marginal maximum likelihood beats the gradient-descent fit by 0.03 on the 25-item COVID knowledge test, by 0.009 on the 30-item ENCCEJA form and the 18-item financial literacy test, and by nothing on the 116-item residency exam. The Denver screener, with 105 items, looks like an exception until one remembers it is age-adaptive: each child answers only the items near their age, about thirty in training, so it is a short test in the sense that matters. Plotting the gap against the number of training responses each person contributes makes the pattern plain. ::: {#cell-fig-gap .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Estimator gap against test length"} gap = imv_tab["mirt_2pl"] n_resp = pd.Series({t: float(data[t][~data[t].test].groupby("pid").size().median()) for t in gap.index}) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6)) ax.scatter(n_resp, gap, s=28, color=[group_colour[GROUP_OF[t]] for t in gap.index]) for t in gap.index: if gap[t] > 0.008: ax.annotate(SHORT[t], (n_resp[t], gap[t]), fontsize=7, xytext=(4, 2), textcoords="offset points") ax.axhline(0, color="0.3", lw=0.8) ax.set(xlabel="median training responses per person", ylabel="IMV of mirt 2PL over PyTorch 2PL") ax.grid(color="0.9", lw=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True) for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-gap-output-1.png){#fig-gap width=649 height=385} ::: ::: Why does it happen? The gap is the estimator, not the optimiser. The companion vignette, [Estimating the 2PL in torch](nn_irt_estimation.qmd), fits the same 2PL in torch by maximum marginal likelihood, integrating the persons out as `mirt` does, and its predictions agree with `mirt`'s to 0.0001 IMV on average. The torch networks here treat each person's $\theta$ as a parameter to be estimated, and the item parameters are then fit around those point estimates. With a dozen or twenty responses per person those estimates are poor, and the item parameters inherit the error, which is the incidental-parameter problem. A prior on $\theta$ alone does not fix it. The companion vignette also shows that fixing the scale of $\theta$ does not close the gap either, and that the alternating joint maximum likelihood fit, the textbook version of this estimator, does worse than the Adam network. The gap is largest on the short tests, so few responses per person make the problem possible. Plug-in prediction (the item curve at $\hat\theta_p$) rather than posterior-predictive prediction does not explain any of it (0.0002 on the Woodworth), so the difference lies in fitting the items. We have left the network as it is so that the effect is visible; it is the price of the simplest possible estimator, and readers who build their own networks should know it is there. ## Limitations - **The held-out set is also the validation set.** Each PyTorch model is reported at its best held-out epoch, which flatters every network by a small amount and the wider ones by slightly more, since they have more epochs at which to get lucky. A third split would fix this; we judged that at 24 tables and five models the bias is small relative to the effects reported, and the direction is known: it works against the 2PL, not for it. - **Two estimators, one model.** The PyTorch 2PL (MAP by gradient descent) and the `mirt` 2PL (marginal maximum likelihood) are the same model and do not give the same held-out loss. The comparison that is fair is therefore networks against the PyTorch 2PL and flexible curves against the `mirt` 2PL, and the page is written that way. The companion vignette shows that an estimator which integrates over the persons closes the gap in torch, and that fixing the scale of $\theta$ does not. - **Only person and item identities enter the model.** The networks see exactly what the classical models see, so this is a comparison of functional forms, not of information. Sequential models of learning [@piech2015dkt] use the order of responses; models with item text as input can predict items never seen in training; variational IRT replaces the point estimates with an encoder network. All of these use more than the (person, item, response) triple, and all can be scored with the same held-out cells and the same IMV, but none is on this page. - **Dichotomous, dense tables only.** The cell-level split and the Bernoulli loss are written for 0/1 responses. Polytomous tables need a different output layer and a different loss; sparse tables raise the question of whether the missingness is informative. - **Subsampling.** Tables are capped at 5,000 respondents and 116 items. The gains reported for the inventories are therefore gains at that size; a wider network may do relatively better with more data, which is the usual pattern and is not tested here. - **Twenty-four tables, chosen by hand.** The groups were picked to span kinds of structure, not sampled from the warehouse, and the counts per group are small. The qualitative pattern (dimension helps where there is one, depth does not) is consistent across the groups; the sizes of the gains are specific to these tables. ## Reproducibility **Source code for this page:** [`nn_irt.qmd`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt.qmd), [`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py), [`nn_irt_chart.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_chart.py) and [`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R).
